To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
BMI is a poor predictor of body fatness and the newly proposed Asia Pacific BMI cutoffs for obesity are appropriate for Taiwanese subjects.
Taiwanese people have a lower BMI but a similar body fat percentage to Caucasians.
Taiwanese subjects had lower body mass index (BMIs) and higher percent body fat (percent BF%) than Caucasians.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the BMI-BF% relationship and the BMI-BF%-related BMI or BF% cutoffs in Taiwanese subjects.

the BMI and BF% cutoffs of obesity in the Taiwanese population and the corresponding cutoffs for Asians in general, and it is hoped that our results will be useful to clinicians, nutritionists, and epidemiologists.

the ethnic differences in the relationships between BMI, BF%, and age in Taiwanese subjects, and the corresponding BF% (25% for male, and 38% for female) for the BMI cutoffs (≥25 k/m2) for obesity in Taiwanese subjects, which may be useful in clinical practice and public health.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BMI cutoffs for obesity should be redefined to 25 kg /m2 in Asian-Pacific populations.
the BMI and BF% are not interchangeable in the Asian population, and the Asian BMI cutoffs for obesity should be redefined by the BF% cutoffs.
the Asian cutoffs of 23 and ≥25 kg/m(2) for overweight and obese, respectively, may be acceptable in the Taiwanese population.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a BMI≥30  kg/m2 in Taiwanese men or a BMI≥25  kg/m2 for both men and women would be equivalent to a BF%≥25% or ≥35% for men and ≥38% for women, respectively.
the Asian BMI cutoff of 23 kg/m 2 is a better predictor of BF% than the Caucasian BMI cutoff of 25 kg/ m 2 in the Taiwanese population.
the BMI of 25 kg m(-2) is equivalent to the BF% of 35% in females, and 25% and 35% are the corresponding BF% cutoffs for BMI of 23 kg m-2 and BMI of 25 kg m(-2), respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the BF% is a more reliable index of obesity than BMI.
a low BMI may not necessarily reflect a low BF%.
the BMI cutoffs for Asian populations may be appropriate, but the BF% cutoffs should not be used for the diagnosis of obesity in Asian populations.
